title: Stop sorting to check anagrams: the tally-sheet reel
caption:
"listen" and "silent": same letters? 🧩
Most people sort both words and compare. That's O(n log n).

Think Scrabble. You wouldn't alphabetize two racks of tiles. You'd keep a tally:
+1 for every tile in the first rack, −1 for every tile in the second.
Every row back at zero means the same tiles.

In code: return False if the lengths differ; counts is the tally sheet (a dict from letter to number); +1 for each letter of s, −1 for each letter of t; then every count must be 0. One pass: O(n).

Our test run on 1,000,000 letters (Python): sorted() 215 ms, Counter 55 ms. Counting took about a quarter of the time.

Warehouses reconcile stock the same way: +1 per box in, −1 per box out.

⚠️ The classic 26-slot array only covers a–z. Give it "café" and Python raises IndexError: list index out of range, while JavaScript quietly returns false. Beyond a–z, count with a hash map.
⚠️ Never compare sets: set("aacc") == set("ccac") is True, but they aren't anagrams. Counts matter.

Your turn: "aab" vs "abb". Which rows miss zero? 👇

Watch every count change on leetExpert, the interactive DSA course. Link in bio.

title: Big-O in 60 seconds — animated carousel

Big-O isn't about seconds. It's about what happens when your input doubles. 📈

O(1): same work. O(n): 2× the work. O(n²): 4× the work.

That last one is the nested loop your AI loves to write. It passes the small tests, then crawls on real data.

title: Two pointers on one card (the real cheatsheet, as a reel and a single image)
caption:
Two pointers, the whole pattern on one card. 📌 Save this.

Sorted array + pair sum → opposite ends: l at the front, r at the back; too small moves l in, too big moves r in.
Remove / move while reading ahead → fast & slow: fast explores, slow marks the end of what you keep.
Area between two lines → move inward, always the shorter side (the taller one can never raise the minimum).
Merge two sorted lists → one pointer each: take the smaller head, then append the rest.

Targets: O(n) time with O(1) extra space; the merge is O(n+m).
⚠️ Opposite ends needs sorted data.
⚠️ Watch l < r: with l <= r the middle element can pair with itself.

title: Two pointers, as a gift card: trace reel (re-cut)
caption:
$15 gift card. Two items. Every cent. 🎁
The menu is sorted: $1 $3 $4 $5 $7 $8 $9.

Trying every pair takes 21 checks. With 1,000 items, it's 499,500.

Two pointers: put one finger on the cheapest item and one on the priciest.
Too low? Even the priciest item can't lift the cheapest one to $15, so cross the cheapest off.
Too high? The priciest item can't fit with anything that's left, so cross it off.

$1+$9, $3+$9, $4+$9, $5+$9, $7+$9 (too high), $7+$8 = $15. That's 6 checks instead of 21: O(n) time, O(1) memory.

Databases join sorted tables the same way (a merge join): one pointer per table, with no nested loop over every pair.

⚠️ It only works on sorted input. Stop when the fingers meet (`left < right`), or you'll buy the same item twice.

title: Watch binary search throw away half
caption:
Find 9 in [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13]. 📖 Do what you'd do with a paper dictionary: open the middle, keep one half, ignore the other.

mid = 7 < 9 → everything up to 7 is too small. Gone.
mid = 11 > 9 → 11 and everything after it. Gone.
mid = 9 → found, in 3 checks.

def binary_search(arr, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(arr) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
        if arr[mid] == target: return mid
        elif arr[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
    return -1

Each check halves the range: O(log n). A million sorted numbers take at most 20 checks. A billion, 30.

⚠️ The classic bug: lo = mid instead of mid + 1. Search [1, 3] for 3: mid stays 0 and lo stays 0, forever.
⚠️ It only works on sorted data, or anything where one comparison tells you which half to drop.

Your turn: how many checks to find 13 in this list? 👇

title: The coach won't give you the answer (inside leetExpert)
caption:
I ran a broken Two Sum on leetExpert. The coach didn't fix it. 👀

Draft: for each number, store it in a map, then check if its partner is there.
Run → 2 of 4 tests pass.

The coach names the case that broke:
"two_sum([3, 2, 4], 6) returned [0, 0]; expected [1, 2]. Open Hint 1."

I swapped the pair and ran again. Now case 1 broke too, so it pointed one step further: Hint 2, "check before insert."

Why [0, 0]? At i = 0 we store 3, then ask whether 6 − 3 is in the map. It is: it's the 3 we just stored. So 3 pairs with itself.
Fix: check first, then store. The map now holds only earlier numbers, so a number can never find itself. 4 of 4. ✅

And the coach still says: "I still will not write the code."

In an interview nobody hands you the fix. You get a failing case and reason your way out.

title: Answer any range sum in O(1): prefix sums as an odometer
caption:
nums = [2, 4, 1, 5, 3]. What's the sum from index 1 to 3? 4 + 1 + 5 = 10.
Now answer 10,000 of those. Adding each range from scratch costs up to O(n) every time.

Think of a car's odometer: it only shows the total since the car was new. Any trip = end reading − start reading. You never re-drive the trip. 🚗

A prefix array is that odometer: 0, 2, 6, 7, 12, 15.

def build_prefix(nums):
    prefix = [0] * (len(nums) + 1)   # prefix[0] = 0, the sum of nothing
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + x
    return prefix

sum(l..r) = prefix[r + 1] − prefix[l]
1..3 → 12 − 2 = 10. 2..4 → 15 − 6 = 9. One subtraction, however wide the range.

Our test run, 10,000 queries on 100,000 numbers (Python): 4.96 s summing each range vs 6.1 ms with a prefix array, build included.

⚠️ Only for an array that doesn't change: update one value and every later total is stale.
⚠️ Off-by-one: prefix[r] − prefix[l] drops nums[r] (7 − 2 = 5, not 10).

Your turn: using just two numbers, what's sum(0..4)? 👇

title: "Next greater element" has a shape: the monotonic stack
caption:
For each number, find the first bigger number to its right: [2, 1, 5, 3]. Checking to the right of every number is O(n²).

Picture a concert 🎤: once someone tall stands in front of you, everyone shorter behind them is blocked for good. Only taller people ever matter again.

The stack keeps the numbers still waiting, biggest at the bottom:
2 arrives → push. 1 arrives → push. 5 arrives → pop 1 (answer 5), pop 2 (answer 5), push 5. 3 arrives → push. At the end, 5 and 3 keep −1.

def next_greater(nums):
    answer = [-1] * len(nums)
    stack = []                      # indexes, not values
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < x:
            answer[stack.pop()] = x
        stack.append(i)
    return answer

Each index goes in once and comes out at most once: O(n). Our test run on 10,000 numbers (Python): 953 ms checking right of each vs 0.6 ms with the stack.

⚠️ The trap: store values instead of indexes, and when you pop you don't know where the answer goes. Look it up with index() and duplicates break it: [1, 1, 3] → [3, −1, −1].

title: This removes the even numbers. Or does it? (remove while iterating)
caption:
An AI wrote this in two seconds. It passes the sample test. Would you ship it? 🤔

for n in nums:
    if n % 2 == 0:
        nums.remove(n)

[1, 2, 3] → [1, 3] ✓
[2, 4, 6, 7] → [4, 7] ✗ (4 is even, and it survived)

Why: the for loop walks by position, and the position moves forward every time. remove() deletes the value and shifts everything after it one step left, so the next item lands in the slot you just checked, and the loop skips it. It's like checking tickets along a row of seats while everyone slides left under your finger.

Fix 1: don't edit the list you're reading. Build a new one:
return [n for n in nums if n % 2 != 0]

Fix 2, in place: a read pointer and a write pointer. Copy each keeper to write and move write forward. Write never passes read, so nothing unread is overwritten. Then del nums[write:].

And even the version that works (loop over a copy, remove from the original) is O(n²). Our test run on 100,000 numbers: 7,972 ms vs 4 ms for the new list.

Python raises "RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration" for a dict. Lists and JavaScript arrays just skip, silently.

Your turn: what does the buggy version return for [1, 2, 2, 3]? 👇

title: If you see "contiguous", think window: the sliding window as an inchworm
caption:
Shortest stretch of [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3] with sum ≥ 7? Trying every start and every end is O(n²).

Picture an inchworm 🐛: the front stretches forward to grab new ground, and when it's overreached, the back pulls in. Neither end ever backs up.

2+3+1 = 6 → grab 2: 8 ✓ (length 4) → pull in: 6 → grab 4: 10 → pull in: 1+2+4 = 7 ✓ (length 3) → pull in: 6 → grab 3: 9 → pull in: 4+3 = 7 ✓ (length 2). Answer: 2.

for right in range(len(nums)):
    total += nums[right]
    while total >= target:
        best = min(best, right - left + 1)
        total -= nums[left]
        left += 1

Both pointers only move forward, so it's O(n) even with a loop inside a loop. Our test run on 10,000 numbers (Python): 848 ms checking every stretch vs 1.18 ms for the window.

⚠️ The trap: write if instead of while and the window shrinks at most once per step. It never gets tight: on this exact list it answers 4, not 2.
⚠️ It needs non-negative numbers. Target 5 on [4, −2, −3, 4, 1]: the window finds nothing, but [4, 1] works.

title: Max sum of k in a row. Looks clean. (the fixed window's missing last window)
caption:
An AI wrote this, and it passes the sample ([2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], k = 3 → 9). Would you ship it? 🤔

def max_sum_k(nums, k):
    best = float("-inf")
    for i in range(len(nums) - k):
        best = max(best, sum(nums[i:i + k]))
    return best

[1, 2, 3, 9], k = 2 → 5. The answer is 12 (3 + 9).
[4, 5], k = 2 → -inf.

Count the windows: a 2-wide frame on 4 numbers fits at starts 0, 1 and 2. That's n − k + 1. range(n − k) stops one short, so the last window is never checked. Fix: + 1.

Second problem: every window is summed from scratch, which is O(n·k). Slide instead: sum the first window once, then add the number entering on the right and subtract the one leaving on the left. O(n).

Our test run, 100,000 numbers with k = 10,000 (Python): 12.35 s summing every window vs 11.7 ms sliding.

Your turn: how many windows of size 3 fit in 10 numbers? 👇

A "Second problem" card reads "k additions × every window = O(n·k)". A second code card walks the sliding version: sum the first window once, add the number entering on the right and subtract the one leaving on the left, keep the best, one add and one subtract per step, O(n). Bars for 100,000 numbers with k = 10,000 show 12.35 s for summing every window against 11.7 ms for sliding. An interview-tell card reads "k numbers in a row? Say 'n − k + 1, then slide'". A challenge asks how many windows of size 3 fit in 10 numbers. A leetExpert lockup ends the reel.

title: Binary search in JavaScript. One character is wrong. (the float `mid`)
caption:
Tested on [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13]: every target found. Would you ship it? 🤔

const mid = (lo + hi) / 2;

Search [2, 4, 6, 8] for 6 → -1. But 6 is right there.

lo = 0, hi = 3 → (0 + 3) / 2 = 1.5. JavaScript doesn't round, so arr[1.5] is undefined. undefined isn't === 6 and isn't < 6, so the code falls into the last branch: hi = 0.5. It never looks at a real index again.

Why did the tests pass? On 7 numbers, lo + hi is even at every step. The bug only hides on lengths 1, 3, 7, 15…: one less than a power of two.

Python's / makes a float too, but it crashes: "TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not float". Loud beats silently wrong.

Fix: const mid = lo + Math.floor((hi - lo) / 2);
It's always a whole index, and it never adds two huge numbers (overflow-safe in Java/C++).

Your turn: 7 hides the bug. What's the next length that does? 👇

Step through every line on leetExpert, the interactive DSA course. Link in bio.

title: Watch recursion go down and come back up (the call stack)
caption:
factorial(3) = 3 × 2 × 1. Here's what the computer actually does. 🥞

Think of cafeteria trays: every call sets a fresh tray on top, and you only ever work on the top one.

Down: factorial(3) waits on factorial(2), which waits on factorial(1), which waits on factorial(0). That's the base case: return 1.
Up: 1 × 1 = 1, pop. 2 × 1 = 2, pop. 3 × 2 = 6, pop. Answer: 6, four frames deep (n + 1).

def factorial(n):
    if n == 0:
        return 1          # the base case, the floor
    return n * factorial(n - 1)   # smaller problem; the multiply waits

Every frame costs memory. Python stops at 1,000: factorial(1000) raises "RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded". JavaScript allows around 10,000.

⚠️ Break the base case (step down by 2: 3 → 1 → −1 → …) and it skips 0 forever. It doesn't hang, it crashes.

Your turn: how many frames deep does factorial(5) go? 👇

Then a call stack builds from the bottom, labelled "winding down: each call waits": frames factorial(3), factorial(2) and factorial(1) each say "waiting: n × ?", and factorial(0) says "base case → 1". The label changes to "unwinding: multiply on the way back". factorial(0) pops, factorial(1) fills in "1 × 1 = 1" and pops, factorial(2) fills in "2 × 1 = 2" and pops, and factorial(3) fills in "3 × 2 = 6" and pops, leaving "factorial(3) = 6" and "4 frames = n + 1". A code card walks factorial line by line: the base case returns 1 (the floor); otherwise n × factorial(n − 1), a smaller problem every call; the multiply waits until the call comes back. A card reads "Every frame costs memory": Python stops at 1,000 frames, factorial(1000) raises RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded, and JavaScript allows around 10,000. A second code card shows broken(n), which steps down by 2: "3 → 1 → −1 → −3 … never 0", not a hang but a crash, RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded. An interview-tell card reads "Space of a recursive function? Say 'O(n), one frame per call'". A challenge asks how many frames deep factorial(5) goes. A leetExpert lockup ends the reel.

title: Fibonacci in three lines. What does fib(30) cost?
